cl-01.title: Chinese and Chinese Characters
explain: **Chinese** (汉语 Hànyǔ) is the language spoken in China and in many other regions. This department treats both learning the language itself (**Chinese linguistics**) and reading texts written in Chinese (**Chinese literature**). This core sequence covers the most basic spoken and written elements. When Chinese appears for the first time, it is accompanied by Hanyu Pinyin and an English meaning.

Chinese has many dialects whose speech differs greatly from region to region. Some differ so much that speakers cannot understand each other. For this reason there is a common standard language, called **Putonghua** (普通话 pǔtōnghuà). Putonghua is what this core sequence teaches.

Chinese is written with **Chinese characters** (汉字 hànzì). One character is usually read as one syllable, and it is generally a word or part of a word with a meaning. This differs from scripts such as the alphabet or Hangul (the Korean script), which record only sound.

Chinese characters come in two systems of forms: **simplified characters** (简体字), made with fewer strokes so as to be easier to write, and **traditional characters** (繁体字), which continue the older forms. Simplified characters are official in mainland China, Singapore, and elsewhere, while traditional characters are widely used in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and elsewhere. Examples of the same character taking different shapes are as follows.
- 马 (simplified) - 馬 (traditional): horse
- 书 - 書: book
- 国 - 國: country
- 门 - 門: door
- 学 - 學: to learn
Not every character differs in shape. Many characters, such as 人, 山, 水, and 大, are the same in simplified and traditional forms. This department writes in simplified characters.

How were Chinese characters created? Traditionally the principles by which characters are formed are divided into six, and at the introductory level it helps to know four of them.
- **Pictograph**: imitates the shape of an object. 日 (sun), 月 (moon), 山 (mountain), 木 (tree).
- **Indicative character (ideograph)**: points to a meaning that is hard to draw as a shape by using dots or lines. 上 (up) and 下 (down), and 本 (root, origin), which adds a mark to 木; 三 shows a number with three horizontal strokes.
- **Associative compound**: combines two or more characters to make a new meaning. 明 (bright), combining 日 and 月; 林 (grove), made of two 木; 休 (to rest), combining 人 and 木; 男 (man), combining 田 and 力.
- **Phono-semantic compound**: combines a part that indicates meaning with a part that indicates sound. In 妈 (mother), 女 (woman) carries the meaning and 马 carries the sound.

explain.alt: A figure showing the four principles of character formation in four rows. The pictograph row: 日, 月, 山, 木. The indicative row: 上, 下, 本, 三. The associative compound row: 明 (日+月), 林 (木+木), 休 (人+木), 男 (田+力). The phono-semantic row: 妈 (女+马), 河 (氵+可), 湖 (氵+胡), 吗 (口+马).

explain: In fact most Chinese characters are phono-semantic compounds. However, the sound component is only a hint. The sound component of 妈, 马, is read mǎ, while 妈 is read mā. The sounds are not identical but merely similar, and in many cases they have drifted apart because pronunciation has changed between ancient times and today. So reading a character by trusting its sound component alone can lead to mistakes.

The part that indicates meaning often serves as the **radical**. 河 (river) and 湖 (lake), which contain 氵 (water), are related to water, and 吗, which contains 口 (mouth), is related to speech and tone. Knowing the radical lets you guess the rough meaning of a character you are seeing for the first time.

examples.title: Growing characters from the same component
body: One 木 is a tree, two 木 make 林 (grove), and three 木 make 森 (sēn, a dense forest). The meaning accumulates as the number of components grows, with the forest getting larger. This is a representative example of the associative compound principle.

As an example of phono-semantic compounds, compare 妈 (mā, mother) and 吗 (ma, a character that marks a question). Both use 马 as the sound component, but their meaning components differ, 女 and 口. So the characters and their meanings differ.

checks.explanation: The key points are that a phono-semantic compound is a meaning component plus a sound component, and that the sound component is only a clue to pronunciation and does not match it exactly.

However, the sound component is only a hint, so it is often just similar to the actual pronunciation rather than identical. Pronunciation has also changed over time, so reading a character by its sound component alone can lead to mistakes.

cl-02.title: Hanyu Pinyin and Tones
explain: It is hard to know the sound of a Chinese character from its shape alone. So there is a notation that writes sounds in the Roman alphabet. This is **Hanyu Pinyin** (汉语拼音 Hànyǔ pīnyīn), or **pinyin** for short. Pinyin is written beside characters in dictionaries and textbooks to show how to read them.

A syllable is usually divided into three parts.
- **Initial**: the consonant at the beginning of a syllable. For example, m in mā.
- **Final**: the vowel part that follows the initial. In mā, a.
- **Tone**: the pitch contour laid over the whole syllable.
Some syllables have no initial. 爱 (ài, to love) has only a final and a tone.

Putonghua has four **tones** and a lightly read **neutral tone**. A tone is how the pitch moves within a syllable, and the same syllable with a different tone becomes a different word. In standard Korean, pitch is not the basic means of distinguishing words, so this feels unfamiliar at first.
- **First tone** (ˉ): continues high and level.
- **Second tone** (ˊ): rises from the middle to high.
- **Third tone** (ˇ): dips low and then rises slightly.
- **Fourth tone** (ˋ): falls sharply from high to low.
- **Neutral tone**: read short and light, and no tone mark is attached.

explain.alt: Tone contours drawn in four panels. Each panel has five dotted lines marking five pitch levels. In the first-tone panel, 妈 mā is a line running horizontally at the very top. In the second-tone panel, 麻 má is a line rising upward from the middle. In the third-tone panel, 马 mǎ is a curve that dips down and then rises toward the top. In the fourth-tone panel, 骂 mà is a line falling from the very top to the very bottom.

explain: The figure divides pitch into five levels from 1 (low) to 5 (high) and shows the movement of each tone as a line. It is usual to describe the first tone as 5 to 5, the second as 3 to 5, the third as falling from 2 to 1 and then rising to about 4, and the fourth as falling from 5 to 1.

Even the same ma splits in meaning according to tone.
- 妈 mā: mother
- 麻 má: hemp (the plant)
- 马 mǎ: horse (the animal)
- 骂 mà: to scold
Sound is not played on this screen. The essential point is that although all of these sound roughly like "ma" to an English speaker, they are distinguished by pitch. Approximating them in English spelling has limits, so learn them from the tone-contour figure and the explanation.

Tone marks are placed above the vowel. When there are several vowels, the usual rule is to put the mark on a if there is an a, and otherwise on o or e. One character is one syllable, so it has one tone. In a doubled character such as 妈妈 (māma, mother), the second syllable is commonly read in the neutral tone, lightly. 爸爸 (bàba, father) is the same.

Tones can also change when words are read together. When two third tones come in a row, the first third tone is read like a second tone. 你好 (nǐ hǎo, hello) is written in pinyin as nǐ hǎo, but in actual speech it is read closer to ní hǎo. Remember that the pinyin for a character is written with its tone from before the change.

examples.title: Breaking down pinyin
body: Let us take 你好 nǐ hǎo apart. nǐ has the initial n, the final i, and the third tone. hǎo has the initial h, the final ao, and the third tone. Because third tones come in a row, the first syllable is read like a second tone.
Let us also read 谢谢 xièxie (thank you). The first syllable xiè is in the fourth tone, and the second syllable is in the neutral tone, so it has no mark.

cl-03.title: Basic Sentences: Word Order and 是, 有, 吗
explain: The basic word order of Chinese is **subject - verb - object** (SVO). In Korean the verb comes at the end, but in Chinese the verb sits between the subject and the object. Also, Korean marks roles with particles such as 가 and 를, whereas Chinese has no such particles, so the **position** where a word is placed tells its role.

Let us first learn the personal pronouns. The basics are 我 wǒ (I), 你 nǐ (you), 他 tā (he), and 她 tā (she). 他 and 她 sound the same and differ only in the character. Adding 们 men makes the plural: 我们 wǒmen (we), 你们 nǐmen (you, plural), 他们 tāmen (they).

The form of the verb does not change with person or tense. In 我喝水 wǒ hē shuǐ (I drink water), 喝 hē stays 喝 even when the subject changes.
- 我喝水。 Wǒ hē shuǐ. I drink water.
- 我爱猫。 Wǒ ài māo. I love cats.
- 我喝茶。 Wǒ hē chá. I drink tea.

**是** (shì) expresses "A is B." 我是学生。 Wǒ shì xuésheng. (I am a student.) To negate it, put 不 (bù) before 是. When a fourth-tone syllable follows 不, 不 is read like a second tone and written bú. So 不是 is bú shì. 我不是老师。 Wǒ bú shì lǎoshī. (I am not a teacher.)
**有** (yǒu) means "to have" or "there is." 我有书。 Wǒ yǒu shū. (I have a book.) The negation of 有 uses **没** (méi), not 不. 我没有书。 Wǒ méiyǒu shū. (I do not have a book.)

A question that can be answered yes or no is made by adding **吗** (ma) to the end of a statement. The word order is not changed. 你是学生吗？ Nǐ shì xuésheng ma? (Are you a student?) 吗 is in the neutral tone. One answers with 是。(Yes) or 不是。(No) or with a full sentence.

explain.alt: A figure dividing two Chinese sentences into boxes. The top row is a statement with 我 (wǒ, subject), 喝 (hē, verb), and 水 (shuǐ, object) placed in order. The bottom row is a question with 你 (nǐ, subject), 是 (shì, verb), 学生 (xuésheng, noun), and 吗 (ma, question) placed in order, and the 吗 box is orange.

explain: At the end of a Chinese sentence, a circle-shaped 。 is used instead of a period. The comma is ，, the question mark is ？, and the exclamation mark is ！. This punctuation takes up one square like a Chinese character.

examples.title: Extending sentences

你是老师吗？ Nǐ shì lǎoshī ma? (Are you a teacher?) - 我不是老师，我是学生。 Wǒ bú shì lǎoshī, wǒ shì xuésheng. (I am not a teacher; I am a student.)

checks.explanation: The key points are that Chinese has SVO word order and position tells the role, whereas in Korean particles tell the role and the verb comes at the end.

In Korean the verb comes at the end of the sentence, and particles such as 가 and 를 are attached to show roles. Chinese has no such particles, so the position where a word is placed determines its role.

cl-04.title: Numbers and Measure Words
explain: First, the numbers from 0 to 10: 零 líng (0), 一 yī (1), 二 èr (2), 三 sān (3), 四 sì (4), 五 wǔ (5), 六 liù (6), 七 qī (7), 八 bā (8), 九 jiǔ (9), 十 shí (10). Approximating them in English spelling has limits, so learn them while also watching the tone marks of the pinyin.

explain.alt: A figure writing ten Chinese numbers in two rows of boxes. The top row: 一 yī 1, 二 èr 2, 三 sān 3, 四 sì 4, 五 wǔ 5. The bottom row: 六 liù 6, 七 qī 7, 八 bā 8, 九 jiǔ 9, 十 shí 10.

explain: From 11 on, the rule is simple. For 11 through 19, the ones digit is attached after 十: 十一 shíyī (11), 十五 shíwǔ (15), 十九 shíjiǔ (19). From 20 up, it is tens digit + 十 + ones digit: 二十 èrshí (20), 二十八 èrshíbā (28), 九十九 jiǔshíjiǔ (99).

In Chinese, when counting things, a **measure word** is inserted between the number and the noun. It is similar to unit words in Korean such as 명 (person), 권 (volume), 마리 (animal), and 잔 (cup). The word order is **number + measure word + noun**. Korean often puts the noun first, as in "학생 세 명" (three students), but in Chinese the number and measure word come before the noun.

These are measure words frequently used at the introductory level.
- **个** (gè): the most common measure word, used broadly for people and many objects. 三个学生 sān gè xuésheng (three students)
- **本** (běn): for books and the like. 三本书 sān běn shū (three books)
- **只** (zhī): for small animals such as cats. 一只猫 yì zhī māo (one cat)
- **杯** (bēi): for things in a cup or glass. 一杯茶 yì bēi chá (one cup of tea)

explain.alt: The title is number + measure word + noun. The top row has three boxes in order: 三 (sān, number), 个 (gè, measure word), 学生 (xuésheng, noun). The bottom row has three boxes in order: 两 (liǎng, number), 只 (zhī, measure word), 猫 (māo, noun).

explain: When counting two, **两** (liǎng) is used instead of 二 before a measure word. 两个朋友 liǎng gè péngyou (two friends), 两只猫 liǎng zhī māo (two cats). But when reading the number itself, or inside numbers such as 12 and 20, 二 is used.

The sound of 一 (yī) changes depending on the tone of the following syllable. Before a fourth tone it is read yí, and before a first, second, or third tone it is read yì. So 一个 is written yí gè, 一本书 yì běn shū, 一只猫 yì zhī māo, and 一杯茶 yì bēi chá. When counting numbers one by one, or when it is the final digit, it is yī.

examples.title: Reading numbers and attaching measure words
body: 五杯水 wǔ bēi shuǐ is five cups of water. 二十五个学生 èrshíwǔ gè xuésheng is twenty-five students. Even as the number grows, the word order stays the same: number + measure word + noun.
没有三本书 means "there are no three books." After 没有 méiyǒu, number + measure word + noun follows.

cl-05.title: Basic Expressions: Greetings and Self-Introduction
explain:
In this lesson we learn the expressions used first in everyday life. Sound is not played, so read using the pinyin and the explanation of tones.
- 你好！ Nǐ hǎo! Hello.
- 早上好！ Zǎoshang hǎo! Good morning.
- 再见！ Zàijiàn! Goodbye, see you again.
- 谢谢。 Xièxie. Thank you.
- 不客气。 Bú kèqi. You are welcome.
- 对不起。 Duìbuqǐ. I am sorry.
- 没关系。 Méi guānxi. It is all right.
To raise the level of politeness by one step, use **您** (nín) instead of 你. 您好！ Nín hǎo! (Hello.) 您 is the polite form used to superiors or to someone you are meeting for the first time.

The basic frame of a self-introduction is as follows.
- 我叫…。 Wǒ jiào… I am called … (my name is …).
- 我是…人。 Wǒ shì… rén. I am a person from … (I am …).
- 很高兴认识你。 Hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ. Nice to meet you.
Putting in a country name gives 我是韩国人。 Wǒ shì Hánguó rén. (I am Korean.) China is 中国 Zhōngguó and Japan is 日本 Rìběn. In Chinese names, the family name comes first and the given name after. For example, in 王明 Wáng Míng, a fictional person of this department, 王 is the family name.

Questions asking for a name or a country are made by putting an **interrogative word** in the place of the part that is not known.
- 你叫什么名字？ Nǐ jiào shénme míngzi? What is your name?
- 你是哪国人？ Nǐ shì nǎ guó rén? What country are you from?
A question with an interrogative word does not change the word order; the interrogative word simply goes into the position of the missing content. And 吗 is not attached to such questions. 吗 is used only for yes/no questions.

explain.alt: A dialogue in four speech bubbles. A says 你好！我叫王明。(Nǐ hǎo! Wǒ jiào Wáng Míng.), B says 你好！我叫李安。(Nǐ hǎo! Wǒ jiào Lǐ Ān.), A says 你是哪国人？(Nǐ shì nǎ guó rén?), and B says 我是韩国人。(Wǒ shì Hánguó rén.), with the English meaning written in each bubble as well.

explain: The figure is a fictional dialogue in which two people meet for the first time and greet each other. Both A and B first say their names, then A asks about the country and B answers.

examples.title: Building my own introduction frame
body: 我叫李安。我是韩国人。 Wǒ jiào Lǐ Ān. Wǒ shì Hánguó rén. This is a sentence in which the fictional person 李安 (Li An) introduces himself. By changing only the name and the country, anyone can introduce themselves with the same frame.

cl-06.title: Reading and Writing a Short Fictional Text
explain:
Let us read a short text using what we have learned so far. Below is a self-introduction written by the fictional person 李安 (Li An). Pinyin and meaning are attached sentence by sentence.
1. 你好！我叫李安。 Nǐ hǎo! Wǒ jiào Lǐ Ān. Hello! My name is Li An.
2. 我是学生，不是老师。 Wǒ shì xuésheng, bú shì lǎoshī. I am a student, not a teacher.
3. 我有一只猫，它叫小白。 Wǒ yǒu yì zhī māo, tā jiào Xiǎo Bái. I have a cat, and its name is Xiao Bai.
4. 我有三本书，也有两个朋友。 Wǒ yǒu sān běn shū, yě yǒu liǎng gè péngyou. I have three books, and I also have two friends.
5. 我喜欢喝茶。你呢？ Wǒ xǐhuan hē chá. Nǐ ne? I like drinking tea. And you?

Let us organize the new words. **它** (tā) is "it," referring to something that is not a person. **也** (yě) means "also, too" and is placed before the verb. **喜欢** (xǐhuan) is "to like," and it can be followed by a verb phrase such as 喝茶 (drink tea). **呢** (ne) is a modal particle that turns back the same question as was just asked, asking "And you?" 小白 Xiǎo Bái is a fictional name given to the cat.

The tip for reading is this. First find the verbs (是, 有, 叫, 喝, 喜欢) to get the skeleton of the sentence, and read what comes before as the subject and what comes after as the object. Next, find the chunks of number + measure word + noun. Finally, cover the pinyin, look only at the characters, and try to recall the meaning. Even if an unknown character appears, the radical can give a clue to the meaning.

Now let us write for ourselves. The card below is a frame that becomes a self-introduction when the blanks are filled in. To the right of each line, the pinyin frame and the English meaning are written.

explain.alt: A self-introduction fill-in card. It has four lines. 我叫 ____ 。(name), 我是 ____ 人。(country), 我有 ____ 。(number + measure word + noun), 我喜欢 ____ 。(verb + noun). To the right of each line are written the pinyin frame and the English meaning.

explain: Here is a checklist for writing. Does the subject come first? Does the verb come before the object? Did you include a measure word when stating a number? Did you use 两 when it is two? Did you put 。 at the end? Adding pinyin and the English meaning makes it easier for the reader to understand.

examples.title: An example with the frame filled in
body: 我叫王明。我是中国人。我有两本书。我喜欢喝水。 Wǒ jiào Wáng Míng. Wǒ shì Zhōngguó rén. Wǒ yǒu liǎng běn shū. Wǒ xǐhuan hē shuǐ. (My name is Wang Ming. I am Chinese. I have two books. I like drinking water.) This is an example written by a fictional person.
Note: in 我有两本书, the number 2 is 两, not 二. In this way, the rules learned earlier work together within a single sentence.

cl-07.title: The Four Complement Types of Modern Chinese and Aspect Particles
explain: Korean and Japanese express the result and aspect of an action through verb endings, but Modern Chinese, an isolating language, combines a **complement** (补语 bǔyǔ) or an **aspect particle** (动态助词) after the predicate (verb or adjective) to express precisely the completion, direction, possibility, and degree of a state. Because word order determines grammatical relations, one must grasp exactly the position of the complement and the rules for combining it with negators.

A **resultative complement** attaches a resulting state (完, 懂, 见, 好, etc.) directly after the verb to indicate the result that the action produced (e.g., `听懂` tīngdǒng, to hear and understand). Since this negates an event that has already been realized, the negator in principle is `没(有)` placed before the verb (`没听懂`). A **directional complement** divides into the simple directional complement, to which `来` (toward the speaker) or `去` (away from the speaker) is attached, and the compound directional complement, in which `来·去` is combined after `进·出·上·下·回·过·起` (e.g., `走进来`, to walk in). A place object must be placed before `来/去` (`走进教室来`).

explain.alt: A table of the four complement types of Modern Chinese (resultative, directional, potential, degree) showing combination structure, example sentences, and function, with a box diagram below of the three aspect particles (了 completion/realization, 着 continuation, 过 experience)
explain.caption: Affirmative and negative forms of the four complements and the aspectual differentiation of the aspect particles

explain: A **potential complement** inserts the structural particle `得` (affirmative) or the negator `不` (negative) between a resultative or directional complement and the verb, to indicate whether the result of the action can be realized (e.g., `听得懂` can understand by listening / `听不懂` cannot understand by listening). A **degree complement**, on the other hand, attaches `得` after the predicate and places after it a phrase expressing degree, evaluating the degree reached by an action or state (e.g., `说得很好` speaks very well). The negation of a degree complement negates the adjective after `得` (`说得不好`).

The three **aspect particles** attached after the verb mark not tense (past, present, future) but the **aspect** of the action. `了` (le) indicates completion or realization of an action (`吃了三碗饭`, ate three bowls of rice), `着` (zhe) indicates continuation of an action or state (`门开着`, the door is open), and `过` (guò) indicates whether there is an experience in the past (`去过北京`, has been to Beijing).

A limitation to note is the pragmatic difference between the potential complement (`V+得/不+R`) and the modal verb (`能/可以+V+R`). The negative form `听不懂` is used very frequently to mean that one simply cannot understand because of subjective or objective circumstances, but there is an asymmetry in that the affirmative form is more often replaced in everyday conversation by the modal verb construction (`能听懂`) than by the potential complement (`听得懂`).

examples.title: Distinguishing the negation of a resultative complement from the negation of a potential complement
body: Situation A: I listened to the lecture yesterday but did not understand the content. Situation B: Chinese is spoken so fast that I simply cannot follow it.

Step 1: In A, the result was not realized at a specific point in time, so the negation of a resultative complement, `没听懂` (méi tīngdǒng), is used. Step 2: In B, which means realization is impossible because of ability or circumstances, the negation of a potential complement, `听不懂` (tīngbudǒng), is used.
Interpretation: when `没` comes before the verb, the result is unrealized; when `不` is inserted between the verb and the complement, the possibility is negated.

examples.title: Compound directional complements and the word order of place objects
body: Combine the verb `走` (to walk), the compound directional complement `进去` (to go in), and the place object `图书馆` (library).
Step 1: A place object must always be positioned before `来/去`. Step 2: Arrange it as `走进图书馆去` (`*走进去了图书馆` is ungrammatical).
Interpretation: an ordinary object can be placed either before or after `去`, but a place object is fixed before `来/去`.

cl-08.title: The Disposal Construction (把), the Passive (被), and Serial-Verb and Pivotal Constructions
explain: The basic word order of Modern Chinese is `subject (S) + verb (V) + object (O)`, but special constructions that move the object before the verb are used to emphasize the result of disposal that an agent exerts on an object, or to topicalize the patient. The representative constructions are the **disposal construction** (把字句) and the **passive construction** (被字句).

The **disposal construction** (`S + 把 + O + V + other element`) indicates that the agent (S) handled the object (O) and changed its position or state. For this construction to hold, three strict syntactic constraints must be met. First, the object of `把` must be a **definite** (定指) noun phrase already known to speaker and hearer. Second, the verb must be a disposal-type transitive verb capable of affecting the object, so perception, psychological, and existential verbs (`看见, 喜欢, 有`, etc.) cannot be used. Third, the verb alone cannot end the sentence, and it must be followed by an **other element** such as a complement, an aspect particle (`了/着`), or a reduplicated form.

explain.alt: A diagram of the word-order formulas of the disposal construction (把 sentence) and the passive construction (被 sentence), in which the object is moved from the basic SVO sentence (他喝了那杯茶), and of the constraints on the position of the negator
explain.caption: Argument movement in the disposal and passive constructions and the constraints on negators and complements

explain: The **passive construction** (`patient + 被 + (agent) + V + other element`) indicates that the object was affected by the action. In written and standard language the agent after `被` can be omitted, as in `那杯茶被喝完了` (that tea has been drunk up), but after the colloquial passive prepositions `叫` (jiào) and `让` (ràng) an agent noun must always be present. In both the disposal and passive constructions, the negators (`没, 不`) and modal verbs are always placed **before** `把` or `被` (`他没把那杯茶喝完`).

Meanwhile, in a **serial-verb construction** (连动句, e.g., `我去图书馆看书`, I go to the library and read), where two or more verb phrases follow one subject, the agent of all actions is the single subject. By contrast, a **pivotal construction** (兼语句, e.g., `老师让我回答问题`, the teacher had me answer the question) differs in syntactic structure from the serial-verb construction in that the object (`我`) of the first verb (a causative verb such as `请, 让, 叫, 使`) also serves as the subject of the second verb (`回答`).

examples.title: Judging the grammaticality of the disposal construction (把字句)
body: Compare the sentences `*他把那本书看了` and `他把那本书看完了`.

Step 1: Both sentences use a definite object (`那本书`) and a transitive verb (`看`). Step 2: However, the second sentence, in which the result of disposal (`完`) is made explicit, fully satisfies the resultativity constraint of the disposal construction better than the first sentence with only the simple perfective `了` (in particular, ending with the verb alone, as in `*他把那本书看`, is absolutely impossible).
Interpretation: the `把` construction describes not the action itself but what resulting state the object has reached.

examples.title: Analyzing the argument structure of serial-verb and pivotal constructions
body: Sentence A: `他买票进场` (He bought a ticket and entered). Sentence B: `妈妈叫他买票` (Mother told him to buy a ticket).

Step 1: In A, the agent of both `买票` and `进场` is `他`, so it is a serial-verb construction. Step 2: In B, the agent of `叫` is `妈妈`, but the agent of `买票` is the object `他`, so `他` is the pivot (both object and subject).
Interpretation: if the first verb has a causative meaning and the semantic subjects of the two verb phrases differ, it is a pivotal construction.

cl-09.title: Function Words, Word Order, and Part-of-Speech Conversion in Classical Chinese (Wenyanwen)
explain: **Classical Chinese** (文言文 wenyanwen), which takes the written language of the pre-Qin (先秦) and Han (两汉) periods as its model, is centered on monosyllabic words, and the grammatical function of vocabulary shifts flexibly with context and word order. Unlike Modern Chinese, it does not use the copula `是` and forms sentences of judgment with the structure `~者, ~也`, while the mood of question, rhetorical question, and conjecture is determined by **function words** (虚词) at the end of the sentence.

Among the core function words, `之` (zhī) performs three functions. First, it is used as a genitive particle ("of," e.g., `先王之道`, the way of the former kings). Second, after a transitive verb it is used as a third-person object pronoun ("it/him," e.g., `学而时习之`, to learn and from time to time practice it). Third, placed between the subject and the predicate, it is used as a structural particle that removes the independence of the sentence and turns it into a nominal clause (e.g., `孤之有孔明`, my having Kongming). Meanwhile, `其` (qí) functions as a third-person possessive ("his/its") or as a conjectural or rhetorical adverb, `者` as a bound noun ("one who does / thing that"), and `所 + verb` as a noun phrase indicating the object of an action ("that which is done").

The most important syntactic rule in reading Classical Chinese is **object inversion** (宾语前置). Ordinarily it takes the `verb + object` order like Modern Chinese, but under two conditions the object moves before the verb. First, when an **interrogative pronoun** (`何, 谁, 安, 奚`, etc.) is the object of a verb or preposition (e.g., `何以` = `以何`, by what). Second, when a **pronoun** is the object in a **negative sentence** (a sentence using `不, 未, 莫, 无`, etc.) (e.g., `不吾知也` = `不知吾也`, does not know me).

In addition, Classical Chinese is rich in **part-of-speech conversion** (词类活用), in which a word's part of speech changes temporarily with context. Representative types include the **causative usage** (使动用法), in which an ordinary noun takes on a causative meaning (e.g., in `生死人而肉白骨`, `肉` is "to make flesh grow on white bones"), the **putative usage** (意动用法), which regards a noun or adjective as being such (e.g., in `不耻下问`, `耻` is "to regard it as shameful to ask those below"), and the usage in which a noun modifies a verb before it like an adverb (e.g., `豕立`, to stand like a pig).

The passive likewise mainly uses the constructions `~于` ("to be ~ed by"), `为~所~`, and `见~于~` instead of the Modern Chinese `被`. Only by combining these three principles, the polysemy of function words, conditional object inversion, and part-of-speech conversion, can one decipher original classical texts precisely without misreading.

examples.title: Reading object inversion of a pronoun in a negative sentence
body: Let us analyze the Analects passage `不患人之不己知` (do not worry that others do not know you).

Step 1: In the clause after `人之`, the negator `不` is used and the object is the reflexive pronoun `己` (oneself). Step 2: By the rule of inversion of a pronoun object in a negative sentence, `己` has moved before the verb `知`, and the original semantic order is `不知己`.
Interpretation: `之`, placed between the subject (`人`) and the predicate (`不己知`), forms the nominal clause "that others do not know oneself."

examples.title: Combining the 所 construction with the passive construction
body: Compare the classical constructions `为天下笑` (to be laughed at by the whole world) and `为仲卿所遣` (to be sent away by Zhongqing).
Step 1: The first sentence expresses the passive with `为 + agent + verb`. Step 2: The second sentence is the typical classical passive formula `为 + agent + 所 + verb`.
Interpretation: `所 + verb` nominalizes the event that became the object of the passive, and `为` introduces the agent.

cl-10.title: The Sources of Pre-Qin and Han Poetry: The Shijing and the Chuci
explain: The history of Chinese classical poetry begins from two sources (the Feng-Sao 风骚 tradition): the **Shijing** (《诗经》, Classic of Poetry), a realistic collection of folk songs and court hymns from the Yellow River basin in the north, and the **Chuci** (《楚辞》, Songs of Chu), born from the romantic mythology and shaman songs of the state of Chu in the Yangtze (Changjiang) basin in the south.

The Shijing, which gathers **305 poems** from the early Western Zhou to the mid-Spring and Autumn period, is the oldest anthology of poetry in China, and it basically takes the form of **four-character lines** (four characters per line) with reduplicated words and repeated stanzas. Its contents divide into three parts: **feng** (风, "airs"; the Airs of the States, 160 poems in 15 states), folk songs of each region; **ya** (雅, "elegantiae"; the Greater and Lesser Elegantiae, 105 poems), banquet and court-audience songs of the Zhou royal house; and **song** (颂, "hymns"; 40 poems), eulogies of ancestral temple sacrifices. To these are added three expressive techniques organized by later poetics: **fu** (赋: narrating facts directly as they are), **bi** (比: comparing by likening to another thing), and **xing** (兴: first chanting of natural objects to evoke poetic mood and association, and then entering the real theme). Together they form the **Six Principles of the Shijing** (六义: feng, ya, song, fu, bi, xing).

By contrast, the Chuci, represented by **Qu Yuan** (屈原) of Chu in the late Warring States period, broke away from the northern refined four-character form and pioneered a form of lines of varying length with long breath. In particular, it brought out impassioned melody by inserting **xi** (兮 xī), a modal particle of the Chu dialect, at the end or middle of lines, and sang of loyalty, anguish, and mythological imagination through the allegory of fragrant plants (香草) and beautiful women (美人). Qu Yuan's masterpiece **"Li Sao"** (《离骚》) is the first long lyric poem in the history of Chinese literature.

By the Han dynasty, **yuefu poems** (乐府诗, e.g., "Peacock Flies Southeast" and "Ballad of Mulan"), folk songs gathered by the Music Bureau, had established the tradition of narrative poetry, and in the late Eastern Han, literati absorbed the **five-character form** of yuefu and left the purely lyrical **"Nineteen Old Poems"** (《古诗十九首》). The maturation of this five-character old-style poetry, through the Wei, Jin, and Northern and Southern Dynasties, became the direct foundation for the birth of Tang regulated verse (jintishi).

In short, the engaged lyricism of the Shijing (the Feng-Ya spirit) and the personal anguish and romantic metaphor of the Chuci served for the next two thousand years of Chinese poetry as the two reference frames by which poets defined their literary identity.

examples.title: Analyzing the 'xing' (兴) technique in "Guan Ju" (关雎) of the Shijing
body: Let us read the opening lines `关关雎鸠，在河之洲。窈窕淑女，君子好逑` ("Guan-guan" cry the ospreys on the river islet. The graceful maiden is a fine match for the gentleman).

Interpretation: this technique of raising the poetic thought by first presenting natural objects is 'xing' (兴) among the Six Principles of the Shijing.

cl-11.title: The Rules of Tang Regulated Verse (Jueju and Lüshi) and Li Bai and Du Fu
explain: The Tang dynasty was the golden age of Chinese poetry, and by developing the tonal theory of the Northern and Southern Dynasties (the theory of the four tones and eight faults), it perfected **regulated verse** (近体诗 jintishi, also called modern-style verse), in which the number of lines, the number of characters, level and oblique tones, rhyme, and parallelism are strictly standardized. This contrasts with the earlier free verse forms, which are called **old-style verse** (古体诗 gutishi, gushi).

Regulated verse divides broadly into the **jueju** (绝句, quatrain: five-character 20 characters, seven-character 28 characters), made of four lines, and the **lüshi** (律诗, regulated verse: five-character 40 characters, seven-character 56 characters), made of eight lines. The jueju takes the four-part composition of **qi, cheng, zhuan, jie** (起承转结: opening, development, turn, conclusion), while the lüshi is grouped in pairs of lines into four couplets: the **opening couplet** (首联 shoulian, lines 1-2), the **second couplet** (颔联 hanlian, lines 3-4), the **third couplet** (颈联 jinglian, lines 5-6), and the **closing couplet** (尾联 weilian, lines 7-8). In particular, **the two middle couplets of the lüshi, the second and third couplets, must form parallelism (对偶) in which parts of speech and semantic structure match in pairs.**

explain: The tonal rules of regulated verse rest on the **level-oblique rule** (平仄法), which divides the four tones of Middle Chinese (level, rising, departing, entering) into two groups for placement: the **level tone** (平声: a low, flat, continuing sound) and the **oblique tone** (仄声: the winding sounds of the rising, departing, and entering tones). Within a couplet, the first line (odd line) and the second line (even line) must be opposite in level and oblique pattern (对 duì), and the second character of the even line of a preceding couplet and the odd line of the following couplet must have the same tone (粘 zhān, "adhesion"). In addition, for **rhyme** (押韵), in principle only **level-tone rhymes** are used, and characters of the same rhyme category are placed at the end of the even lines (lines 2, 4, 6, 8; line 1 is optional), keeping **a single rhyme throughout** (一韵到底: unified under one rhyme to the end).

In the poetic world of the High Tang, the romantic "Poet Immortal" (诗仙) **Li Bai** (李白) and the realist "Poet Sage" (诗圣) **Du Fu** (杜甫) stood as twin peaks. Li Bai excelled in yuefu, old-style (gufeng) poems, and the jueju, and sang of the liberation of the individual with bold imagination and natural melody. Du Fu, by contrast, poured the grim social reality and the suffering of the people before and after the An Lushan Rebellion into the somber and precise **lüshi** form, and was credited with **shishi** (诗史), meaning "history in verse," achieving a perfect union of formal beauty and social consciousness.

examples.title: Analyzing the parallelism of the second and third couplets of Du Fu's five-character lüshi "Spring View" (春望)
body: Second couplet (lines 3-4): `感时花溅泪，恨别鸟惊心` (Grieving over the times, even flowers draw tears; hating the parting, even birds startle the heart).

Step 1: `感时` (verb-object) matches `恨别` (verb-object), `花` (noun) matches `鸟` (noun), and `溅泪` (verb-object) matches `惊心` (verb-object), so parts of speech and syntactic structure correspond exactly one to one. Step 2: In tone as well, the first line (`平平平仄仄`) and the second line (`仄仄仄平平`) form a precise opposition.
Interpretation: the second couplet (lines 3-4) and the third couplet (lines 5-6) of the lüshi must form strict parallelism (对偶) in this way.

examples.title: Calculating the character count of regulated verse and the required number of rhymes

Interpretation: old-style verse can change rhyme midway (huan yun), but regulated verse uses only one level-tone rhyme from beginning to end.

cl-12.title: Song Ci: Tune Patterns, Irregular Lines, and the Graceful and Bold Schools
explain: If the literature representing the Tang dynasty is the refined five- and seven-character regulated verse (Tang poetry), the verse form representing the Song dynasty is the **ci** (词, Song ci 宋词), which started from the lyrics of popular banquet music (燕乐 yanyue) and settled as literati poetry. Because ci is a literature in which characters are fitted to the melody of a piece of music, it is also called **tianci** (填词, "filling in words"), and because the number of characters in each line varies long and short with the tune, it has the alias **changduanju** (长短句, "long and short lines").

In composing a ci, the poet does not make up the form arbitrarily but must choose a **cipai** (词牌, tune pattern: for example "Pusa Man," "Yu Meiren," "Shuidiao Getou," "Niannu Jiao"), which is both the name of an established tune and a framework of rules. For each cipai the total number of characters, the sections (the two-part structure of the upper and lower halves, etc.), the characters per line, the level and oblique tones, and the rhyme positions are strictly specified. In the early period the name of the cipai was itself the theme, but by the Song dynasty the cipai came to mean only the purely musical and metrical form, and the actual title (词题) was added separately. By length, those of 58 characters or fewer are classed as **xiaoling** (小令, short pieces), 59 to 90 characters as **zhongdiao** (中调, medium pieces), and 91 characters or more as **manci** (慢词, slow or long pieces).

By aesthetic style, Song ci developed broadly in two currents, the **graceful school** (婉约派 wanyue) and the **bold school** (豪放派 haofang). Following **Li Yu** (李煜), the last ruler of the Southern Tang in the Five Dynasties period (masterpiece "Yu Meiren"), **Liu Yong** (柳永) of the Northern Song laid the foundations of the graceful school by expressing the bustle of the city and the poignant sorrow of parting between lovers in long-breathed manci and plain language. Afterward, **Li Qingzhao** (李清照), a woman ci poet of the late Northern Song and early Southern Song, wielded the delicate baimiao (白描, plain line-drawing) technique and reduplicated characters (叠字: `寻寻觅觅，冷冷清清，凄凄惨惨戚戚`) to raise the aesthetic of graceful ci to its peak.

However, the person who broke the common notion that "ci must carry only delicate and tender feelings (词别是一家)" was **Su Shi** (苏轼, Dongpo) of the Northern Song. Su Shi practiced **yi shi wei ci** (以诗为词: composing ci in the manner of composing shi poetry), bringing historical reflection, philosophical detachment, and spirited nature into the domain of ci, and thereby founded the **bold school** (masterpieces "Niannu Jiao: Reminiscing at Red Cliff" and "Shuidiao Getou"). In the Southern Song, **Xin Qiji** (辛弃疾, Jiaxuan), who sang of patriotic loyalty and the recovery of northern territory seized by the Jin, succeeded Su Shi and perfected bold ci, so the two are named together as **Su-Xin** (苏辛).

In short, if Tang poetry speaks for balanced architectural beauty and the public aspiration of the scholar-official (expressing intent, 言志), Song ci began from fluent musical undulation and the delicate curves of the private inner life (expressing feeling, 缘情) and finally became a stylistic expansion that also embraced historical and philosophical thought.

examples.title: Classifying cipai by length and judging their rules
body: Classify Li Yu's "Yu Meiren" (56 characters in all), Su Shi's "Shuidiao Getou" (95 characters in all), and Liu Yong's "Yulin Ling" (103 characters in all) by character count (xiaoling 58 or fewer, zhongdiao 59 to 90, manci 91 or more).

Step 1: "Yu Meiren," at 56 characters, is 58 or fewer, so it is a 'xiaoling' (小令). Step 2: "Shuidiao Getou" at 95 characters and "Yulin Ling" at 103 characters are both 91 or more, so they belong to the long tunes, 'manci' (慢词).
Interpretation: after Liu Yong and Su Shi of the Northern Song, long-breathed manci became truly popular, and ci's capacity for narrative and thought broadened greatly.

examples.title: Contrasting the diction and style of the graceful school (Li Qingzhao) and the bold school (Su Shi)
body: Line A: `大江东去，浪淘尽，千古风流人物` (Su Shi, "Niannu Jiao: Reminiscing at Red Cliff"). Line B: `寻寻觅觅，冷冷清清，凄凄惨惨戚戚` (Li Qingzhao, "Sheng Sheng Man").

Step 1: A is typical of the bold school, unfolding the vast waves of the Yangtze and the heroes of a thousand ages on a grand scale of space and time. Step 2: B is the essence of the graceful school, placing 14 reduplicated characters one after another to draw the intimate undulations of loss and solitude.
Interpretation: even within the same long-and-short-line form, completely different aesthetic effects are created by the choice of diction and the combination of tones.

cl-13.title: The Tang-Song Classical Prose Movement and the Prose Aesthetics of the Eight Great Masters
explain: From the Wei, Jin, and Northern and Southern Dynasties to the early Tang, the mainstream prose of the Chinese literary scene was **parallel prose** (骈俪文 pianliwen, also siliu bianwen, "four-six parallel prose"), which splendidly matched parallelism in lines of four and six characters and concentrated on tonal patterns and ornament of allusions (典故). But parallel prose revealed the limitation that, bound by formal beauty, it was hard for it to carry substantive thought or social criticism.

In response, **Han Yu** (韩愈) and **Liu Zongyuan** (柳宗元) of the Mid-Tang period launched the **Classical Prose Movement** (古文运动), which sought to break the formalist parallel prose and return to **guwen** (古文, "ancient prose"), the free and unadorned prose style of the pre-Qin (先秦) and Han (两汉) periods. Their central ideal was **wen yi zai dao** (文以载道, or wen yi ming dao 文以明道), that is, "writing should be a vessel that carries the Way (Confucian principle and real-world truth)." However, their "return to the past" did not mean copying ancient characters as they were, but a stylistic innovation of discarding stale clichés (**chen yan wu qu** 陈言务去) and writing original and vivid prose in every sentence.

Han Yu unfolded majestic and forceful argument in essays ("On Teachers," "On the Way"), while Liu Zongyuan, through landscape travel writings composed in exile ("Eight Records of Yongzhou") and fables ("The Snake-Catcher's Tale"), combined sharp social satire with limpid descriptions of nature. In the Mid-Tang literary world, the guwen style also met fictional narrative and helped the flourishing of **Tang chuanqi** (传奇: classical-language short stories, e.g., "Yingying's Story," "Li Wa's Story"), as well.

When parallel prose regained force in the late Tang and Five Dynasties period, **Ouyang Xiu** (欧阳修) in the mid-Northern Song, as leader of the literary world, reignited the Classical Prose Movement and finally established guwen as the firm orthodox style of Chinese prose. Ouyang Xiu presented plain, fluent prose with deep resonance ("Record of the Old Drunkard's Pavilion"), and from his circle and influence emerged **Su Xun** (苏洵), **Su Shi** (苏轼), and **Su Zhe** (苏辙), the father and two sons (the Three Sus, 三苏), along with **Wang Anshi** (王安石) and **Zeng Gong** (曾巩).

When Mao Kun (茅坤) of the later Ming dynasty compiled the *Selected Prose of the Eight Masters of Tang and Song*, bundling two of the Tang (Han Yu, Liu Zongyuan) and six of the Song (Ouyang Xiu, Su Xun, Su Shi, Su Zhe, Wang Anshi, Zeng Gong), the name **Eight Great Masters of Tang and Song** (唐宋八大家) was established. Tang-Song guwen served for the following thousand years as the standard norm of prose in the East Asian Chinese-character cultural sphere.

examples.title: Comparing the style and function of parallel prose and Tang-Song guwen
body: Feature A: obligatory four- and six-character parallelism, harmony of level and oblique tones, centered on ornate rhetoric. Feature B: free line length, oriented to 'wen yi zai dao' (writing that carries the Way), flexible integration of argument, narrative, and lyricism.

Step 1: A is the parallel prose (siliu prose) that was popular from the Six Dynasties to the early Tang. Step 2: B is the Tang-Song guwen advocated by Han Yu and Liu Zongyuan and perfected by Ouyang Xiu and Su Shi.
Interpretation: the Classical Prose Movement was not a mere imitation of an old style but a practical and aesthetic prose reform that restored the expression of thought and the narrative function.

body: Passage: `古之学者必有师。师者，所以传道受业解惑也` (Learners of old surely had teachers. A teacher is one by whom the Way is transmitted, learning is imparted, and doubts are resolved).

Step 1: Unbound by four-six parallelism, it defines the concept clearly with a sentence of judgment (`师者，…也`) and the `所以` (means/reason) construction. Step 2: It directly criticizes the custom of the scholar-officials of the day, who were ashamed to keep a teacher.
Interpretation: this is a model of guwen showing how 'wen yi zai dao' and 'chen yan wu qu' are realized in an actual argumentative essay.

cl-14.title: The Four-Act-Plus-Wedge Structure of Yuan Zaju and Ming-Qing Chuanqi Drama
explain: Following Tang poetry and Song ci, the literary form representing the Yuan dynasty is **yuanqu** (元曲). Yuanqu encompasses sanqu (散曲), lyrical songs composed by literati, and **Yuan zaju** (元杂剧, northern-style zaju), complete dramatic scripts performed on stage. In particular, Yuan zaju is the first full-fledged classical drama form in China, in which song, dialogue, and acting are organically combined.

Yuan zaju has very strict formal rules. A play is basically composed of **four acts** (四折 si zhe: corresponding to today's four acts, forming a structure of opening, development, turn, and conclusion), and when needed a **wedge** (楔子 xiezi: meaning "wedge"), one short interlude that supplements the plot at the introduction or between acts, is added, giving the **four-acts-plus-one-wedge** (四折一楔) structure. Within one act (折) it uses a **single suite of one mode** (一宫调一套曲), which ties together several tune patterns belonging to the same mode (tonality), and rhymes with one rhyme from beginning to end.

There are three elements of stage performance. The first is **chang** (唱), the songs sung to the melody; the second is **binbai** (宾白: spoken lines, with bai for monologue and bin for dialogue), the everyday dialogue exchanged by characters; and the third is **kefan** (科范, shortened to ke 科), the stage directions for the actor's gestures, expressions, and stage movements. Roles are divided into four types: **mo** (末, the male lead is zhengmo 正末), **dan** (旦, the female lead is zhengdan 正旦), **jing** (净), a villain or a role in imposing make-up, and **chou** (丑), the clown. The most distinctive rule of Yuan zaju is the **one-singer-per-play** (一剧一主唱) principle: across all four acts, either only the male lead (zhengmo) sings alone, called **moben** (末本), or only the female lead (zhengdan) sings alone, called **danben** (旦本), and the other roles can only speak lines (binbai).

The supreme masterpieces of Yuan zaju are considered to be the tragedy **"The Injustice to Dou E"** (《窦娥冤》) by **Guan Hanqing** (关汉卿) (a danben sung by the zhengdan, in which the grievance of Dou E, a filial wife unjustly executed, is proven by three supernatural vows including snow in June) and **"The Romance of the Western Chamber"** (《西厢记》) by **Wang Shifu** (王实甫) (a work depicting the love of Zhang Sheng and Cui Yingying in an unconventional long form of five books and twenty acts).

In the Ming and Qing periods, **chuanqi** (传奇), long dramas based on southern music (nanqu and kunqu), flourished (e.g., Tang Xianzu's *The Peony Pavilion*, Hong Sheng's *The Palace of Eternal Youth*, Kong Shangren's *The Peach Blossom Fan*). Ming-Qing chuanqi broke Yuan zaju's limit of four acts and the constraint of a single singer, allowing a long structure of dozens of **chu** (出: acts) and solos and choruses by all roles, and brought a rich stage art to bloom.

examples.title: Analyzing the form and roles of the Yuan zaju "The Injustice to Dou E"
body: Guan Hanqing's "The Injustice to Dou E" consists of an introductory wedge (楔子) and four main acts (折), and the songs (唱) of the whole play are sung by the heroine Dou E (zhengdan 正旦) alone.
Step 1: The structure follows the Yuan zaju standard, 'four acts plus one wedge.' Step 2: Because a single zhengdan is solely in charge of the songs (唱) of all acts, it is a 'danben' (旦本) zaju.
Interpretation: the other characters (the judge Tao Wu, Zhang Lüer, etc.) cannot sing and carry the play only with binbai (dialogue) and kefan (movement).

examples.title: Comparing Yuan northern-style zaju and Ming-Qing southern-style chuanqi
body: Form A: fixed four acts plus one wedge, one mode maintained within an act, the principle of a single singer, zhengmo or zhengdan. Form B: a long play of roughly 30 to 50 chu (出), modulation possible within an act, singing and chorus allowed for all roles.
Step 1: A is the northern-centered Yuan zaju (northern-style). Step 2: B is chuanqi (传奇), the long drama centered on southern kunqu in the Ming and Qing periods.
Interpretation: the condensed dramatic tension of Yuan zaju evolved in Ming-Qing chuanqi into polyphonic and splendid long stage plays.

cl-15.title: The Development of Ming-Qing Chapter Novels and the Narrative Structure of Dream of the Red Chamber
explain: The **huaben** (话本), scripts that storytellers (说话人) told to the public in the entertainment districts (washe, goulan) of Song and Yuan cities, blossomed in the Ming and Qing periods into the vernacular full-length novel in which a long story is divided into dozens to hundreds of **chapters** (回) with a two-line title in parallelism (**huimu** 回目) before each chapter, that is, the **chapter novel** (章回小说 zhanghui xiaoshuo).

In the Ming dynasty, the **Four Great Marvelous Books** (四大奇书) were born, in which literati compiled folk tradition and historical and mythological legend. They are **Luo Guanzhong**'s historical romance **Romance of the Three Kingdoms** (《三国志演义》; semi-classical, semi-vernacular style, late Yuan to early Ming), **Shi Nai'an**'s heroic chivalric novel **Water Margin** (《水浒传》; establishing the vernacular spoken style), **Wu Cheng'en**'s novel of gods and demons **Journey to the West** (《西游记》; mid-Ming), and **Jin Ping Mei** (《金瓶梅》; by Lanling Xiaoxiaosheng), the forerunner of the novel of manners (世情) in which, breaking away from the collective transmission of history, heroes, and myth, an individual author realistically created the everyday life and desires of a merchant family. Later, in the Qing period, the literati satirical novel **The Scholars** (《儒林外史》) by Wu Jingzi and the classical-language short story collection **Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio** (《聊斋志异》) by Pu Songling were added.

explain.caption: The diachronic genealogy of Chinese narrative and dramatic literature and the core structure of Dream of the Red Chamber

explain: The summit of Chinese classical fiction is **Dream of the Red Chamber** (《红楼梦》, original title *Shitou Ji*, The Story of the Stone 《石头记》), written by **Cao Xueqin** (曹雪芹) during the Qianlong era of the Qing. The extant standard edition of Dream of the Red Chamber has **120 chapters** in all; **the first 80 chapters were written by Cao Xueqin** in his lifetime, and **the last 40 chapters were supplemented and published by Gao E** (高鹗) and Cheng Weiyuan. Since the Qing, Dream of the Red Chamber is counted in place of Jin Ping Mei, so that Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Water Margin, Journey to the West, and Dream of the Red Chamber are the **Four Great Classical Novels of China** (四大名著).

Set against the rise and fall of the noble Jia family (贾氏: the Rong and Ning mansions), Dream of the Red Chamber depicts with finesse the tragic love triangle of the protagonist **Jia Baoyu** (贾宝玉), who rejects ritual propriety and success through the examinations, **Lin Daiyu** (林黛玉), his pure soulmate, and **Xue Baochai** (薛宝钗), who conforms to feudal norms, as well as the beauty and ruin of the young women known as the **Twelve Beauties of Jinling** (金陵十二钗). In particular, the **true-false (真假) double structure** that contrasts the Jia family (贾, a homophone of 假 "false") with the Zhen family (甄, a homophone of 真 "true"), the philosophical reflection on form (色) and emptiness (空), and the lively Beijing vernacular style show the peak of Chinese classical realism and tragic aesthetics.

examples.title: The narrative shift from the Ming Four Great Marvelous Books to Jin Ping Mei and Dream of the Red Chamber
body: Compare the mode of creation and subject matter of Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Water Margin, and Journey to the West with those of Jin Ping Mei and Dream of the Red Chamber.

Step 1: The first three are collectively layered narratives re-created from historical records or folk tales and huaben accumulated over a long time. Step 2: Jin Ping Mei and Dream of the Red Chamber are novels of manners (世情) in which the author observed the family and social everyday life of his own time and conceived them originally.
Interpretation: this means that the central axis of the novel shifted from the extraordinary world of heroes and myth to the intimate daily life and psychology of ordinary people and families.

examples.title: Analyzing the chapter composition of Dream of the Red Chamber and the 'true-false' (真假) device
body: Read the division of authorship across the 120 chapters of the standard edition of Dream of the Red Chamber and the line `假作真时真亦假` in Chapter 1 (when false is taken for true, true becomes false as well).

Step 1: Of the 120 chapters, the first 80 were written by Cao Xueqin and the last 40 were continued by Gao E. Step 2: The protagonist's family name `贾` (jiǎ) has the same pronunciation as `假` (jiǎ, false), and the counterpart figure's name `甄` (zhēn) has the same pronunciation as `真` (zhēn, true), questioning the boundary between reality and illusion.
Interpretation: the theme that the glory of the family is like a brief dream (the red chamber dream) is structured through the phonological ambiguity of the characters' names.

cl-16.title: The May Fourth Vernacular Literature Revolution and Lu Xun's Critique of the National Character
explain: In the early twentieth century, amid the collapse of the feudal empire and the invasion of the Western powers, Chinese intellectuals held that to overcome the national crisis, both the classical written language (文言文) cut off from the masses and Confucian feudal thought had to be reformed at the same time. The New Culture Movement arose on the stage of the magazine **New Youth** (《新青年》), founded by Chen Duxiu (陈独秀) in 1915, and it exploded into the **1917 literary revolution** and the **1919 May Fourth Movement**.

In January 1917, **Hu Shi** (胡适) published "**A Preliminary Discussion of Literary Reform**" (《文学改良刍议》) in New Youth, setting out the 'eight don'ts' (八不主义: do not use allusions, do not match parallelism, do not imitate the ancients, and so on) and proposing that the colloquial **vernacular** (白话文) be made the orthodox language of literature. The next month **Chen Duxiu**, in "**On the Literary Revolution**" (《文学革命论》), issued a radical manifesto calling for the overthrow of aristocratic literature, classical literature, and hermit literature and the building of the literature of the common people, realist literature, and social literature. Thereby the historical linguistic shift from the classical language to the vernacular (**unification of speech and writing**) was accomplished.

The master who proved this theoretical manifesto with the first modern creative works was **Lu Xun** (鲁迅, real name Zhou Shuren 周树人), the father of modern Chinese literature. Studying medicine during his years in Japan, Lu Xun realized that a people whose bodies are healthy but whose spirits are numb cannot be saved, and changed direction to literature (abandoning medicine for literature, 弃医从文). In **1918** he published in New Youth **A Madman's Diary** (《狂人日记》), the first full-fledged vernacular short story in modern Chinese literature. Borrowing the form of the diary of a person with persecution delusions, he read the characters **'eat people' (吃人: cannibalism)** between the lines of thousands of years of history books filled with Confucian 'benevolence and morality,' and so directly denounced the violence of feudal ritual propriety.

In the novella that followed, **The True Story of Ah Q** (《阿Q正传》, 1921-1922), Lu Xun dissected, through the day-laborer peasant **Ah Q** of the rural village of Weizhuang (未庄) in the period of the Xinhai Revolution, the sick national character of the Chinese, that is, the **spiritual victory method** (精神胜利法: an attitude of rationalizing in one's mind that one has won even while being defeated and humiliated in reality, lording it over the weak and cringing before the strong). Lu Xun's first story collection **Call to Arms** (《呐喊》, 1923) and second story collection **Wandering** (《彷徨》, 1926, including "The New Year's Sacrifice") show both the passion of enlightenment and the lonely reflection of the intellectual.

The depth of Lu Xun's literature lies in the fact that it did not stop at the enlightener looking down on the masses from above, but never ceased a painful self-reflection that the narrator and intellectual, 'I,' may also be an accomplice of the feudal cannibalistic system ('Perhaps I too ate some of my little sister's flesh').

examples.title: The 'cannibalism' (吃人) metaphor and narrative point of view in A Madman's Diary
body: A Madman's Diary takes a double frame structure: a short 'preface' written in the classical language (from the point of view of a normal friend) and a main text of 13 entries written in the vernacular (from the first-person diary point of view of the madman).

Step 1: In the main text the madman sees through to the essence of cannibalism (吃人), the eating of people, in his family, his neighbors, and the 'benevolence and morality' of the history books. Step 2: But in the preface it is noted calmly in the classical language that the madman recovered from his illness and took up a post as a candidate for a local official.
Interpretation: through the irony that the awakened madman was incorporated once again into the 'normal' bureaucratic system, it doubly criticizes the firm power of the feudal order to absorb.

examples.title: The working mechanism of the 'spiritual victory method' in The True Story of Ah Q
body: After being beaten by ruffians, Ah Q mutters, 'Let us take it that I was beaten by my son,' and falls asleep satisfied with himself.

Step 1: He does not face the humiliation and defeat of objective reality. Step 2: By an imaginary reversal of hierarchy, he manufactures a psychological superiority and extinguishes his own will to resist.
Interpretation: Lu Xun shaped Ah Q not as a specific class but as a universal type of servile self-deception that pervaded the whole semi-feudal, semi-colonial society.

cl-17.title: The Differentiation of Modern Literature in the 1920s-30s: Realism, Romanticism, and the Jing and Hai Schools
explain: In 1921, just after the May Fourth literary revolution, the camp of China's new literature differentiated into two representative literary schools over the social role and aesthetic orientation of literature: the **Literary Association** (文学研究会), formed in Beijing by Mao Dun (茅盾), Zhou Zuoren, Zheng Zhenduo, and others, and the **Creation Society** (创造社), formed by Guo Moruo, Yu Dafu, and others, who had studied in Japan.

The Literary Association raised the banner of **'art for life' (为人生)**, took in nineteenth-century European realism, and led 'problem fiction' and realist literature that objectively record the suffering of the lower classes and social contradictions. The Creation Society, by contrast, at first professed **'art for art's sake' (为艺术)** and sang of romantic liberation of the self and emotional passion (Guo Moruo's poetry collection Goddesses, Yu Dafu's short story "Sinking"). But going through the National Revolution and social upheaval of the mid-1920s, the Creation Society too turned to 'revolutionary literature' and in 1930 formed, together with Lu Xun and others, the **League of Left-Wing Writers** (Zuolian).

Entering the 1930s, modern Chinese novels and drama reached a golden age. **Mao Dun** (茅盾), in his novel **Midnight** (《子夜》, 1933), analyzed the structural limits of Chinese national capital from the macro viewpoint of social science through the bankruptcy of the financial and industrial capitalist Wu Sunfu (吴荪甫) in the semi-colonial metropolis of Shanghai. **Ba Jin** (巴金), in the novel **Family** (《家》, the first part of the Torrent trilogy), denounced with ardent humanitarian passion how the feudal extended-family system destroys the lives and loves of the young generation. Among the achievements of this period are also **Lao She**'s (老舍) **Camel Xiangzi** (《骆驼祥子》; Rickshaw Boy), which depicts Beijing's common society and the tragic degradation of the rickshaw puller Xiangzi (祥子) in vivid Beijing colloquial (jingwei 京味), and **Cao Yu**'s (曹禺) four-act tragedy **Thunderstorm** (《雷雨》), which raised modern Chinese spoken drama (huaju) to a world-class level.

At the same time, in the literary scene of the 1930s the contrast between two regional and aesthetic schools that kept their distance from politically ideological literature stood out: the **Jing school** (京派: centered on Beijing) and the **Hai school** (海派: centered on Shanghai). **Shen Congwen** (沈从文), the leading writer of the Jing school, in his novella **Border Town** (《边城》, 1934), restored in a poetic style the pastoral human nature and the pure beauty of nature untainted by modern civilization, through Cuicui (翠翠), the ferryman's granddaughter in the frontier village of Chadong (茶峒) in Hunan.

The Hai school (the New Sensationists Mu Shiying, Liu Na'ou, and others), which grew up against the urban popular culture of the Shanghai concessions, and the 1940s Shanghai literary genius **Eileen Chang** (张爱玲 Zhang Ailing; representative works "Love in a Fallen City" and "The Golden Cangue"), dissected, instead of grand discourse, the desolate underside of desire, money, and the psychology of men and women inside the declining old extended family, with a delicate yet cold sensibility, and so gave dimension to the spectrum of modern Chinese literature.

examples.title: Contrasting the views of literature of the Literary Association and the early Creation Society
body: Position A: 'Literature is a mirror of the age and must reflect the blood and tears of life (art for life).' Position B: 'Literature springs from inner impulse and self-expression and is not subordinate to utilitarian aims (art for art's sake).'
Step 1: A is the realist line of the Literary Association led by Mao Dun and others. Step 2: B is the romantic line of the early Creation Society led by Guo Moruo, Yu Dafu, and others.

Interpretation: the competition and dialogue of the two schools became the driving force by which China's new literature of the 1920s absorbed realist social inquiry and romantic liberation of individuality at the same time.

examples.title: Comparing the space and aesthetics of Mao Dun's Midnight and Shen Congwen's Border Town
body: Work A (Midnight): the Shanghai stock exchange and textile mills of 1930, comprador capital and labor disputes. Work B (Border Town): a ferry crossing on a frontier river in Hunan, the simple daily life of the grandfather and his granddaughter Cuicui.

Step 1: Midnight is the peak of the social-analysis novel, dissecting the total contradictions of big-city capitalism. Step 2: Border Town is a representative lyrical novel of the Jing school (京派), exploring healthy humanity through a pastoral countryside outside the political whirlwind.
Interpretation: the Chinese novel of the 1930s cultivated side by side the achievements of two poles, macro social realism and lyrical pastoral aesthetics.

cl-18.title: The Development of Contemporary Literature after 1949: Scar, Root-Seeking, and Avant-Garde Literature
explain: In the history of Chinese literature, the period from the 1917 literary revolution up to the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949 is called **modern literature** (现代文学), and the period from 1949 to today is called **contemporary literature** (当代文学). From 1949 until the end of the Cultural Revolution in 1976, the literary scene was dominated by socialist realism, which put political propaganda and class struggle first, following the principle of 'literature and art serving workers, peasants, and soldiers' set out in Mao Zedong's "Talks at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art" (1942).

With the end of the Cultural Revolution (1966-1976) in 1976 and the start of Reform and Opening-up in 1978, Chinese contemporary literature met an explosive thaw (**New Period literature**). The first door was opened by the **scar literature** (伤痕文学) of 1977-1979. This current, which began with Lu Xinhua's (卢新华) short story "Scar" (1978) and Liu Xinwu's (刘心武) "The Class Teacher," denounced in tears the physical and mental wounds left on intellectuals, youth, and families by the ultra-leftist line during the ten years of the Cultural Revolution, and called for the rehabilitation of humanism. Soon after appeared **reflection literature** (反思文学, Wang Meng, Lu Yanzhou, and others), which reflected on the tragedy of the Cultural Revolution as a matter of bureaucratism and historical structure beyond personal misfortune, and **misty poetry** (朦胧诗: Bei Dao, Shu Ting, Gu Cheng, and others), which resisted the darkness of the age.

By the mid-1980s (around 1985), in the awareness that literature must not remain only a political denunciation, two lines of aesthetic innovation arose. The first is **root-seeking literature** (寻根文学), led by Han Shaogong (韩少功), A Cheng (阿城), Jia Pingwa, Mo Yan, and others. They sought to re-excavate the deep archetypes ('roots') of national culture lying outside the Confucian central culture, such as Chu culture, Daoism and Chan, and frontier folk customs, and to reflect culturally and anthropologically on the Chinese way of life and thought.

The second is **avant-garde literature** (先锋文学), led in the late 1980s by **Yu Hua** (余华), Su Tong (苏童), Ge Fei (格非), Ma Yuan, and others. The avant-garde writers dismantled the existing causal plot and the realist theory of reflection and concentrated on **'how to write' (experiments in narrative form) rather than 'what to write'**: exposing the fictionality of the narrator, fragmenting time, and cold and cruel narratives of violence.

After the 1990s, the avant-garde writers stepped back from extreme formal experiment and moved to a mature narrative that gazes at the survival and suffering of ordinary people in history. **Yu Hua**, in the novels **To Live** (《活着》, 1992) and **Chronicle of a Blood Merchant** (《许三观卖血记》, 1995), depicted with restrained sorrow and humor the lives of the common people Fugui (福贵) and Xu Sanguan, who endured turbulent modern history simply by 'surviving,' while **Mo Yan** (莫言) won the **2012 Nobel Prize in Literature** through works such as *Red Sorghum*, *Big Breasts and Wide Hips*, and *Frog*, which combine folk tales and magical realism on the stage of Gaomi Northeast Township (高密) in his native Shandong.

examples.title: The deepening of problem awareness from scar literature to root-seeking and avant-garde literature
body: Stage 1 (1978 scar literature): 'How unjustly did we suffer during the Cultural Revolution?' (denunciation of political harm). Stage 2 (1985 root-seeking literature): 'Why was such a tragedy repeated in the soil of our culture, and what are the deep archetypes of national culture?' (the search for cultural roots). Stage 3 (1987 avant-garde literature): 'How should we dismantle and reconstruct the existing realist language and the grammar of narrative itself?' (experiments in narrative form).

Interpretation: in the ten years after Reform and Opening-up, Chinese contemporary literature evolved rapidly from political liberation to cultural reflection, and again to the acquisition of autonomy of language and form.

examples.title: The change in narrative attitude in Yu Hua's To Live (活着)
body: Compare Yu Hua's avant-garde stories of the late 1980s ("On the Road at Eighteen," "One Kind of Reality") with the 1992 novel To Live.

Step 1: The early avant-garde stories concentrated on cold violence and experiments in narrative technique. Step 2: To Live conveys, in a plain and restrained first-person frame narrative, the voice of the old man Fugui, who after going through the civil war, the Great Leap Forward, and the Cultural Revolution loses his entire family and yet plows a field with a single old ox.

Interpretation: this is a case in which the restrained gaze of avant-garde literature combined with the universal theme of the tenacious vitality of the Chinese people and achieved popularity and artistry at once.

cl-19.title: Bachelor's Capstone I: Chinese Syntax, Classical Chinese Reading, and Synthesis of Poetic Rules
explain: In the first capstone lesson of the bachelor's course in Chinese language and literature, we cross-apply the analytical tools of **Chinese linguistics** (Modern Chinese complements and special constructions, and Classical Chinese grammar) learned in stages 2-5 and **Chinese literature** (rules of classical poetry and the history of classical and modern prose and fiction), to read original texts and syntactic data with precision.

First is the **comparison of object and argument placement** in Modern Chinese and Classical Chinese. Modern Chinese, in its basic SVO order, uses the preposition `把` to pull the object before the verb when emphasizing a change in the state of the object (`S + 把 + O + V + R`), and uses `被` to express the passive. Classical Chinese (wenyanwen), by contrast, even without the preposition `把`, inverts the object before the verb in the case of a **pronoun object in a negative sentence** (`不吾知`) or an **interrogative pronoun object** (`吾谁欺`), and marks the passive with the structure `为 + agent + 所 + verb`. Contrasting the conditions of word-order shift in the two eras makes the continuity and discontinuity of the history of Chinese syntax vivid.

Second is the **combined reading of classical poetic rules and classical constructions**. Because the second couplet (lines 3-4) and the third couplet (lines 5-6) of Tang regulated verse (five- and seven-character lüshi) form strict parallelism (对偶), the part-of-speech conversion of a line (causative, putative, adverbial use of a noun) or an omitted element can be inferred through the corresponding position in the paired line (对文). In this way, linguistic part-of-speech analysis and the poetics of parallelism and level-oblique tones become two wings that verify each other in reading classical texts.

Third is the **diachronic verification of stylistic change**. The transition from the classical prose of the pre-Qin and Han periods and the guwen of the Eight Great Masters of Tang and Song (wen yi zai dao), to the binbai of Yuan zaju and the early modern vernacular of the Ming-Qing chapter novel (Dream of the Red Chamber), and then to the modern vernacular opened up by the 1917 May Fourth literary revolution and Lu Xun's A Madman's Diary, was not a mere change of writing medium but a structural change that altered the whole of literature's audience class, narrative point of view, and way of perceiving reality.

Through the examples and the synthesis questions below, let us carry out together the conversion of Modern Chinese constructions, the reading of Classical Chinese inversion and the passive, and the calculation of character counts and rules of regulated verse and Song ci.

examples.title: Converting a Classical Chinese sentence into Modern Chinese disposal and passive constructions
body: Convert the Classical Chinese passive sentence `茶为客所饮` (the tea was drunk by the guest) into a Modern Chinese passive sentence (`被`) and a disposal sentence (`把`), respectively.

Step 1 (passive conversion): `为 + noun + 所 + V` corresponds to Modern Chinese `被 + noun + V + resultative complement/了`, and following the constraint against ending with the verb alone, a resultative complement such as `完` is supplemented, rendering it as `那杯茶被客人喝完了`.
Step 2 (disposal conversion): Take the agent `客人` as the subject and place the definite object `那杯茶` after `把`, composing `客人把那杯茶喝完了`.

examples.title: Reverse-inferring Classical Chinese grammar through lüshi parallelism
body: Analyze the second couplet `明月松间照，清泉石上流` (the bright moon shines between the pines, the clear spring flows over the rocks) of Wang Wei's five-character lüshi "Autumn Evening in the Mountains" (山居秋暝).

Step 1: Lines 3 and 4 are the second couplet, so they form parallelism. `明月` (noun phrase) matches `清泉` (noun phrase), `松间` (locative noun phrase) matches `石上` (locative noun phrase), and `照` (verb) matches `流` (verb), one to one.

Step 2: Through the parallelism we can also confirm that `松间` and `石上`, with the preposition `于` omitted, are a word order peculiar to Classical Chinese in which a locative modifies the verb (`照, 流`) before it like an adverbial.

cl-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone II: Integrated Criticism of Language, Form, and Era in Chinese Literary Texts
explain: The final capstone task of Lesson 20 is to choose one major text in the history of Chinese literature (or two texts from different eras) and write a critical essay that integrates three layers: **(1) linguistic and stylistic features, (2) generic and formal rules, and (3) the social and intellectual context of the era and the awareness of theme**.

Good Chinese literary criticism does not stop at summarizing the plot or theme of a work impressionistically but derives the theme from the **formal and linguistic evidence of the text**. For example, if one is to criticize Du Fu's lüshi, one must analyze how the fine parallelism of the second and third couplets and the tension of level and oblique tones support the sorrow of wartime reality ('history in verse'); and if one is to criticize Cao Xueqin's Dream of the Red Chamber, one must argue how the phonological symmetry of Jia (贾=假) and Zhen (甄=真) and the Beijing vernacular dialogue give dimension to the fall of a noble family and the tragedy of its women.

Likewise, in dealing with Lu Xun's A Madman's Diary or The True Story of Ah Q, one must show how the contrast of point of view between the classical-language preface and the vernacular main text, or the satirical figuration of the 'spiritual victory method,' interlocks with the historical task of anti-feudal enlightenment in the May Fourth period and with the intellectual's self-reflection. When choosing Yu Hua's To Live or the works of Mo Yan as well, one must point out how avant-garde narrative technique or folk-tale fantasy literarily sublimated the violence of modern history.

It is recommended that the critical essay be composed in the following five steps. **[1. Definition of the text under analysis, its era, and its genre] -> [2. Analysis of language, style, and formal devices] -> [3. Core theme and character and narrative structure] -> [4. Literary-historical significance or comparison with the forms of earlier or later eras] -> [5. The text's limits or modern reinterpretation]**. This task is not automatically scored; after submission, check for yourself through the checklist whether your criticism has the rigor of a bachelor's level.

examples.title: An example of designing an integrated critique: comparing Du Fu's lüshi and Lu Xun's vernacular fiction
body: Theme: the difference in how the 'spirit of critique of reality' is embodied in classical verse and in modern prose in Chinese literature.

Step 1 (analysis of language and form): Du Fu recorded the An Lushan Rebellion ('history in verse') within the strict parallelism and level-oblique rules of the classical language and the eight-line lüshi, whereas Lu Xun in 1918, in A Madman's Diary, exposed the 'cannibalism' of feudal ritual propriety through the bold forms of the vernacular and the first-person diary.

Step 2 (significance and limits): Du Fu maximized poetic completeness within the Confucian framework of loyalty to the ruler and love for the people, while Lu Xun fundamentally doubted the Confucian order itself and called forth the modern subject.

Did I assess the position of the work within the literary-historical context of before and after?
